narrativeReportMd:
## StructureMap R4 to R6 assessment

The R6 `StructureMap` counterpart is present with the same canonical URL, type, kind, derivation, and `DomainResource` base. The resource is not renamed, split, merged, or removed.

Material local breaks are concentrated in the mapping-rule content model and required StructureMap terminology. R4 maps using `source.defaultValue[x]`, `target.contextType`, `dependent.variable`, `group.typeMode = 'none'`, or `target.listMode = 'collate'` will not validate unchanged as R6 StructureMap instances. R6 also introduces valid maps that R4 cannot cleanly represent, including typed date/time transform parameters, root constants, optional/anonymous rules, and the new `target.listMode = 'single'` code.

The highest-risk migrations are semantic, not just syntactic: `contextType='type'`, `listMode='collate'`, non-string default values, and dependent group arguments need manual review or an explicit compatibility policy. Inherited base-artifact changes were intentionally excluded from findings.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: `StructureMap` has multiple local R4-to-R6 breaking changes. The top migration concerns are removed/replaced rule syntax (`defaultValue[x]`, `target.contextType`, `dependent.variable`), required terminology changes (`typeMode='none'`, `listMode='collate'`), and R6-only features that cannot be emitted as standard R4. The main uncertainty is exact intended runtime equivalence for old `collate` versus new `single` and for type-oriented target contexts.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Treat StructureMap migration as a map-language migration rather than a simple JSON rename. Rewrite removed elements, review required code changes, run transformed maps through the intended StructureMap engine, and separately define downgrade behavior for R6-only constants, date/time parameters, empty groups, and anonymous rules.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for validation and wire-format findings because they come directly from local R4/R6 StructureDefinition snapshots and bound CodeSystems. Confidence is lower for exact runtime equivalence of some semantic changes because official narrative diffs, ConceptMaps, and engine execution tests were not available.

findings.title: source.defaultValue[x] was replaced by a string-valued source.defaultValue

oldState.summary: R4 has a polymorphic defaultValue[x] choice under rule.source, serialized with type suffixes such as defaultValueString or defaultValueBoolean.
oldState.narrativeMd: The R4 property is a FHIR choice element and therefore carries the datatype in the JSON/XML member name.

newState.summary: R6 has a non-polymorphic source.defaultValue element of type string.
newState.narrativeMd: The R6 property name is defaultValue without a type suffix and the value domain is a string.

facts.oldValue: many FHIR primitive and complex datatypes

impact.impactRationaleMd: A raw R4 instance with any defaultValue<Type> property uses an element name that does not exist in R6. Non-string defaults are also outside the R6 type domain. R6 string defaults can be downgraded to R4 defaultValueString, but that still requires an explicit property rename.

justification.inferredGoal: Align rule source default values with textual StructureMap mapping syntax rather than arbitrary FHIR typed literals.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain `defaultValue[x]` at least for legacy string defaults, or keep the broader R4 choice as deprecated while preferring R6 string defaults.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal of aligning defaults with textual StructureMap syntax is reasonable, and a scalar string default is simpler for R6 engines. The break is not completely avoidable unless R6 keeps either the R4 choice-shaped wire name or the broad R4 literal domain, both of which materially weaken that simplification.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best less-breaking base design would have kept `defaultValue[x]` as a deprecated compatibility shape, possibly limiting new authoring guidance to `defaultValueString` or string-equivalent values. That would preserve many R4 maps and could preserve all R4 maps only by continuing to accept arbitrary typed defaults. The tradeoff is duplicate or over-broad same-resource representations and unresolved execution semantics for non-string typed defaults.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: A string-only legacy choice preserves only common cases, while preserving all typed R4 defaults keeps a broad or duplicated representation that R6 was trying to simplify.

evidence.detail: R4 defines the source default as a broad choice element.
R6 defines the source default as a string element.
Computed diff showed the R4 choice element removed and the R6 string element added.

examples.examplesMd: defaultValueString can usually be renamed to defaultValue. Boolean, Coding, CodeableConcept, Reference, Quantity, and other non-string defaults need semantic review before conversion.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 removes the general FHIR choice-shaped source default and keeps only a string default. This is a hard validation and serialization break for R4 instances that use typed default values.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R6 StructureDefinition validator rejects legacy defaultValueBoolean/defaultValueCodeableConcept/etc. as unknown elements, and rejects direct non-string values on defaultValue. Code generators change from a choice-discriminated property family to a scalar string property.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Scan source rules for defaultValue* members. Convert defaultValueString to defaultValue. For every other suffix, decide whether the R6 map should use a string literal, a new const, a transform parameter, or custom preprocessing.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A tolerant importer can accept old suffixes and emit warnings, but a strict R6 instance cannot preserve arbitrary R4 typed defaults without extensions or out-of-band metadata.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 allowed `StructureMap.group.rule.source.defaultValue[x]` as a broad choice, while R6 narrows the base element to a single string-valued `defaultValue`. An R4 map that used a typed default such as an integer, boolean, date, or Coding would need a transform or expression rewrite before it validates or runs as an R6 map. That is a real path-level migration break, but the affected resource was R4 FMM 2/trial-use and local core examples did not show this pattern. The R6 design appears to favor expression/text-based map defaults over carrying the full FHIR primitive/complex choice set in the map metadata, so preserving every old typed default in the base model would keep a large and probably underused type surface.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `StructureMap.group.rule.source.defaultValue[x]` has many FHIR choice types.
R6 StructureDefinition: `StructureMap.group.rule.source.defaultValue` is `string`.
Targeted local R4 StructureMap example search did not find `defaultValue[x]` use.
Supplied maturity context: R4 StructureMap FMM 2, trial-use.
freshReview.fmmEffect: R4 FMM 2/trial-use is neutral under the framework: it does not erase the old-valid/new-invalid break, but it lowers the stability burden compared with mature or normative content.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: R4 instances using non-string `defaultValue[x]` properties are outside the R6 element shape and require conversion before validation or execution.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: A less-breaking base design could have retained `defaultValue[x]`, or at least retained the old choice with deprecation. That would preserve old maps but would also keep broad typed default semantics in a map language that R6 appears to simplify to string expressions; the tradeoff is material rather than obviously low cost.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree: the existing report is right that this is a hard type-domain break and that a compatibility-preserving alternative is possible, but I would soften the concern because the path is FMM 2/trial-use and no local examples showed use of typed defaults.

findings.title: target.contextType was removed and target.context became variable-oriented string context

oldState.summary: R4 target.contextType distinguishes type and variable contexts and is required by invariant when target.context is present.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: The R4 binding is removed because the element is removed.

constraints.human: If there is a context, there must be a contextType

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 target.context is an id and the companion contextType declares whether it names a type or a variable.

newState.summary: R6 removes contextType. target.context remains but is string typed and described as the variable this rule applies to.
newState.narrativeMd: The R4 discriminator is gone, and target.context no longer has id lexical constraints.

facts.oldValue: Type or variable this rule applies to

impact.impactRationaleMd: This change affects strict instance validation and also changes what generated models or StructureMap engines can represent. Old instances using the removed shape fail in R6, while R6 instances using the new shape require an explicit downgrade policy for R4.

justification.inferredGoal: Simplify target assignment context to variable-oriented mapping syntax.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep `target.contextType` optional and deprecated, defaulting omitted values to `variable` while still validating legacy `type` and `variable` codes.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 variable-oriented target context goal is understandable, but the local evidence does not show that removing the discriminator was necessary. R4 instances with `contextType='variable'` could have remained valid with deterministic normalization, and even `contextType='type'` could have been handled as a deprecated legacy semantic rather than a validation failure.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base R6 design could have widened `target.context` to string, made `contextType` optional, and specified that omitted `contextType` means `variable`. Existing R4 maps would continue to validate, while R6 authors could omit the field. The cost is carrying a legacy type/variable distinction and requiring engines to define how old `type` contexts are interpreted or rejected at execution time.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: This leaves a legacy discriminator and two ways to say the common variable case, but the ambiguity is manageable and preserves R4 maps during transition.

evidence.detail: R4 includes target.contextType with required map-context-type binding.
R6 omits contextType and changes target.context from id to string.
R4 contextType vocabulary supported the removed discriminator.
Computed diff showed contextType removed and target.context semantics changed.

examples.examplesMd: The simple variable case may migrate by dropping contextType. A contextType='type' target needs map-level review because R6 no longer carries that discriminator.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 no longer serializes or validates target.contextType and narrows the meaning of target.context to a variable context. This invalidates common R4 target fragments and changes how target context semantics are inferred.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: A strict R6 validator treats contextType as an unknown element. A strict R4 validator rejects an R6 target with context but no contextType. R6 string contexts can also be lexically invalid for the R4 id type.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For each target, drop contextType only when it is 'variable' and the context value is still meaningful. For contextType='type', rewrite the map to create or bind the target explicitly using R6 variable-based syntax and verify execution behavior.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: An R6 parser could ignore contextType as a legacy field, but silently doing so for type contexts risks changing transform output. A downgrade converter must choose a contextType and may need to normalize context values to R4 id syntax.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Local R4 examples in the package use target.contextType, increasing confidence that this affects real R4 maps.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 target contexts carried both `target.context` and required `target.contextType` to say whether the context named a type or a variable. R6 removes `contextType` and changes the target context semantics toward a string variable. Existing R4 maps that say `contextType = variable` become structurally invalid even though their meaning can often be preserved by simply dropping the redundant discriminator. Maps that used `contextType = type` need a more semantic rewrite. Because the old element was required whenever context was present, this is a direct wire-format/API break on a central StructureMap target construct, and the common `variable` case looks avoidable.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `StructureMap.group.rule.target.contextType` is bound to `type | variable` and R4 invariant `smp-2` requires it when `target.context` is present.
R6 StructureDefinition: no `target.contextType` element; `target.context` is a `string` described as `Variable this rule applies to`.
R4 core examples `StructureMap-example.json` and `StructureMap-supplyrequest-transform.json` both use `contextType: variable`.
Supplied maturity context: R4 StructureMap FMM 2, trial-use.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral, so I do not treat the break as automatically unacceptable. The path is still central to executable map targets, and local examples show use.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid and runtime/API/codegen: R4 maps with `target.contextType` fail the R6 structure and generated model property expectations; dropping or rewriting the discriminator is needed before engines can process the R6 form.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: A plausible less-breaking base design is to keep `contextType` as optional/deprecated, accepting `variable` as equivalent to omission and defining a clear migration for `type`. That preserves the common R4 wire form with little duplication because the element is only a discriminator for the adjacent context.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree: the existing report's high concern and less-breaking-alternative judgment are directionally right, though the fresh rationale emphasizes the avoidable `variable` case and the local R4 examples rather than the whole resource.

findings.title: dependent.variable was replaced by dependent.parameter

oldState.summary: R4 dependent rules pass group-call arguments through a repeating string variable element.
oldState.narrativeMd: The R4 model is an ordered list of variable names or string-like argument tokens.

newState.summary: R6 removes variable and adds repeating dependent.parameter, content-referenced to the target.parameter backbone with typed value[x] choices.
newState.narrativeMd: The R6 model uses parameter objects rather than raw strings.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The elements share the same dependent parent and cardinality, but the value model changed enough that this should be treated as replacement rather than a trivial rename.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This change affects strict instance validation and also changes what generated models or StructureMap engines can represent. Old instances using the removed shape fail in R6, while R6 instances using the new shape require an explicit downgrade policy for R4.

justification.inferredGoal: Unify dependent group call arguments with target transform parameters.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Add `dependent.parameter` while retaining `dependent.variable` as a deprecated alias for simple variable-reference arguments.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Unifying dependent group-call arguments with the target parameter model is a reasonable R6 design goal because it supports typed arguments and shared transform semantics. Keeping the old string list would reduce validation breakage for simple calls, but it would leave engines and validators with two argument models and incomplete coverage of R6's richer parameter shape.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A compatibility design could have allowed `dependent.variable` for legacy variable names and `dependent.parameter` for the new typed parameter backbone, with an invariant preventing both forms from being mixed ambiguously. This would preserve many R4 instances, but long-term interoperability would suffer from duplicate representations and converters would still need policy for typed R6 parameters that have no R4 variable-list equivalent.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The alias would preserve simple R4 calls but duplicate ordered argument representations and cannot express all R6 typed literal parameters.

evidence.detail: R4 defines dependent.variable as a repeating string.
R6 defines dependent.parameter using the target.parameter content model.
Computed diff showed the variable element removed and parameter added.

examples.examplesMd: The migration example assumes variables are valid id-like variable references. Literal strings or other typed arguments need a different value[x] choice.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 replaces dependent variable passing with a parameter model. This is both a wire-format change and an execution-model change for dependent group calls.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R6 validation rejects dependent.variable as unknown and requires dependent.parameter when a dependent component is present. R4 validation rejects dependent.parameter because the element does not exist.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Rewrite each dependent.variable entry to dependent.parameter. Use valueId when the old value is a variable identifier; use valueString or another value[x] type only when the mapping language semantics require a literal typed parameter. Preserve ordering.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A bidirectional converter can preserve simple variable-name calls, but R6 typed parameters cannot be represented in R4 without degrading them to strings or using extensions.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 represented dependent group call arguments as repeatable strings in `group.rule.dependent.variable`; R6 replaces that with `group.rule.dependent.parameter`, reusing the target parameter backbone and its typed `value[x]`. Existing R4 maps must rename and re-shape each argument before they validate as R6. The migration is usually mechanical for simple variable names, but can require policy if a string was being used ambiguously as a variable name versus a literal or expression. The R6 model is more consistent with other StructureMap parameter handling, so the break looks proportionate despite the real migration work.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `StructureMap.group.rule.dependent.variable` is `1..* string`.
R6 StructureDefinition: `StructureMap.group.rule.dependent.parameter` is `0..*` and content-references `StructureMap.group.rule.target.parameter`.
R6 target parameter uses typed `value[x]` choices, so this is more than a simple wire-name rename.
Supplied maturity context: R4 StructureMap FMM 2, trial-use.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral: it supports accepting a coherent model cleanup when the migration burden is narrow and mostly mechanical.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid and runtime/API/codegen: R4 `variable` array entries are not valid R6 dependent arguments and generated code must use the new `parameter` backbone.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: R6 could have kept `variable` as a deprecated alias for the simple variable-name case, but that would duplicate the new typed parameter representation and require conflict rules if both old and new forms appear. The alternative is feasible but not clearly better for the base model.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree: the existing report correctly sees a hard mapping-shape change and a possible partial compatibility design, but I would not rate it as needing renewed design attention because the R6 parameter model has a coherent goal and the alias alternative has real duplication costs.

findings.title: group.typeMode no longer permits required-binding code 'none'

oldState.summary: R4 group.typeMode is mandatory and required-bound to map-group-type-mode with codes none, types, and type-and-types.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: R4 local CodeSystem concepts are none, types, and type-and-types.

newState.summary: R6 group.typeMode is optional and required-bound to map-group-type-mode with only types and type-and-types.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: R6 appears to represent the old non-default case by omitting typeMode.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Because the binding is required, R4 instances with typeMode='none' fail R6 code validation. Local R4 example StructureMap resources use typeMode='none'. R6 omission can often be downgraded to R4 'none', but that assumes omission has the same semantics.

justification.inferredGoal: Model absence of default type-mode behavior with element absence rather than an explicit none code.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep code `none` in the required binding as a deprecated synonym for omitted `group.typeMode` while making the element optional.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Representing the non-default case by absence is cleaner, but removing the required-binding code `none` creates a direct validation break for R4 maps. The same R6 goal could have been met by allowing omission for new content while still accepting the old explicit code as deprecated.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The less-breaking base design is straightforward: R6 could set `group.typeMode` to 0..1 and keep `none` in the value set with a definition such as "deprecated synonym for absence". Validators and engines could normalize `none` to absence. The main tradeoff is that deprecated representations may persist indefinitely, but this is a small enum-level duplication rather than a conflicting data model.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: There would be two representations for a non-default group, but the synonym is deterministic and has low interoperability cost.

evidence.detail: R4 requires group.typeMode.
R6 makes group.typeMode optional.
R4 CodeSystem includes 'none'.
R6 CodeSystem omits 'none'.

examples.examplesMd: Dropping typeMode is the likely R6 shape for old non-default groups, but map engine behavior should be checked before automated migration.

findings.narrativeMd: The explicit R4 'none' group type mode code is gone in R6, and the element became optional. Required binding semantics make this a hard code validation break for R4 maps that contain 'none'.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R6 validation fails because 'none' is no longer in the required value set. R4 validation fails for an omitted typeMode because R4 requires the element. R6-to-R4 downgrade must choose a value, likely 'none' for omitted typeMode.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Replace typeMode='none' by omitting group.typeMode in R6, subject to manual review that the group is not intended as a default type mapping. Preserve 'types' and 'type-and-types' unchanged.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A compatibility parser could accept 'none' as a legacy synonym for absence, but standards-based R6 required-binding validation will still report it unless compatibility handling is explicit.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 required every group to carry `group.typeMode`, and the code system included `none` for groups that were not default type mappings. R6 makes `typeMode` optional and removes the `none` code. This invalidates ordinary R4 maps that explicitly set the required R4 value `none`, even though the R6 representation appears to express the same state by omission. Because this looks like a mechanical cleanup from required sentinel code to optional absence, R6 could likely have preserved the old wire form while still encouraging omission.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `StructureMap.group.typeMode` is `1..1` with required binding to `map-group-type-mode`.
R4 CodeSystem `map-group-type-mode` includes `none`, `types`, and `type-and-types`.
R6 StructureDefinition: `group.typeMode` is `0..1`; R6 CodeSystem removes `none`.
R4 core examples both use `typeMode: none`.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral, but the path was mandatory in R4 and local examples show the removed code was a normal representation, so the compatibility mechanism matters more than low maturity.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: R4 maps with `typeMode = none` use a required-bound code that no longer exists in R6 and must be transformed to omission.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: A low-cost less-breaking design would keep `none` as a deprecated synonym for absence, or permit it with guidance to omit it in new maps. That avoids invalidating the mandatory R4 sentinel without preserving a complex obsolete model.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree: the existing report's hard-break concern and `Yes` less-breaking-alternative direction match the fresh path-level assessment.

findings.title: target.listMode removes 'collate' and adds 'single' in a required binding

oldState.summary: R4 target.listMode is required-bound to map-target-list-mode with first, share, last, and collate.

newState.summary: R6 target.listMode is required-bound to map-target-list-mode with first, share, last, and single.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: No official ConceptMap was available locally to prove collate and single are equivalent.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This change affects strict instance validation and also changes what generated models or StructureMap engines can represent. Old instances using the removed shape fail in R6, while R6 instances using the new shape require an explicit downgrade policy for R4.

justification.inferredGoal: Revise target list assembly semantics for shared or singular target instances.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Add `single` while retaining `collate` as a deprecated code if its R4 execution semantics can still be supported safely.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The code-system delta is clear, but the local artifacts do not explain why `collate` had to be removed or whether `single` is intended to replace it. Because list modes affect execution, accepting both codes is not a cost-free synonym strategy, yet outright removal is not clearly justified by the available evidence.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design could have kept `collate` in the required value set as deprecated and added `single` for the new behavior. That would preserve R4 maps using `collate` during R4-to-R6 validation. The alternative is only partial because engines would need to preserve or explicitly constrain old `collate` semantics, and the new `single` code would still require separate downgrade policy for R4.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Retaining `collate` preserves R4 validation but may force engines to carry retired list-assembly behavior and does not solve R6-to-R4 representation of `single`.

evidence.detail: R4 CodeSystem includes collate.
R6 CodeSystem omits collate and adds single.
R4 listMode uses the required binding.
R6 listMode uses the required binding.

examples.examplesMd: The R4 example also includes contextType, a separate finding. The listMode-specific issue is that collate is no longer valid in R6 and single is not valid in R4.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 changes the required target list-mode vocabulary. Because listMode guides target collection assembly, the change has both validation and execution implications.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Validators enforce required code membership. Execution engines may also branch on the code, so old engines will not understand 'single' and new engines will not understand 'collate' unless they implement compatibility behavior.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Inventory uses of listMode. Preserve first/share/last. For collate, review intended target-list behavior and choose an R6 representation explicitly. For R6-to-R4, decide whether single can be approximated or must be rejected as non-representable.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: No lossless backward-compatible encoding exists in the standard R4/R6 element without a compatibility code map or extension.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 permitted `target.listMode = collate`; R6 removes `collate` and adds `single`. The published code definitions do not make this a safe rename: R4 `collate` says to reuse the first list item and keep adding content, while R6 `single` describes sharing target instances generated by another rule. A map using `collate` therefore needs an engine-level semantic decision, not just a textual code replacement. Since list assembly affects transformation output, a removed required-bound code with unclear replacement semantics deserves standards review unless there is stronger rationale elsewhere.
keyEvidence: R4 CodeSystem `map-target-list-mode` includes `collate`: `re-use the first item in the list, and keep adding content to it`.
R6 CodeSystem `map-target-list-mode` removes `collate` and adds `single`: sharing target instances generated by another rule.
The binding is required in the StructureMap target list-mode path.
Targeted local R4 StructureMap examples did not show `listMode: collate`, so prevalence was not established from local core examples.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral and prevents assuming broad deployment from the break alone, but transformation list semantics are directly executable and migration may require expert judgment.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid and runtime/API/codegen: R4 maps using `collate` fail R6 terminology validation and engines cannot safely infer whether `single` is the intended behavior.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: A less-breaking base design could retain `collate` as deprecated, or explicitly define `single` as an alias if that was the intent. Retaining a list assembly mode may carry engine burden, but the current evidence does not show that the burden outweighs preserving old maps.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree: the existing report is right to flag a high-impact terminology break and only a partial alternative, but the fresh review treats the exact semantics of `collate` versus `single` as the key reason for renewed review.

findings.title: Rule source min/max cardinality validation was tightened

oldState.summary: R4 source.min is integer and source.max is string without local StructureMap invariants enforcing max syntax or min <= max.

newState.summary: R6 source.min is unsignedInt and R6 adds local error constraints requiring numeric-or-star max and min <= numeric max.

constraints.expression: min.empty() or max.empty() or (max = '*') or iif(max != '*', min <= max.toInteger())
constraints.human: Min cardinality must be less or equal to max cardinality
Max SHALL be a number or '*'

facts.newValue: min <= max when max is numeric
max must be a non-negative integer string or '*'

impact.impactRationaleMd: A structurally R4-valid instance could carry a negative source.min, a non-numeric source.max, or min greater than numeric max and pass the older shape. R6 makes those invalid. These are probably data-quality defects, but strict validation is tighter.

justification.inferredGoal: Formalize cardinality sanity checks that were implicit in the transformation semantics.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No equivalent less-breaking base design was identified for enforcing valid source cardinality semantics.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: R4 already described `source.max` as a number or `*`, and negative or inconsistent cardinalities are semantically invalid for executable map rules. R6 makes those expectations computable with an unsigned minimum and error constraints. The break mainly affects structurally accepted but nonsensical R4 content.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The obvious less-disruptive option would be warning-only validation, but that is migration leniency rather than an equivalent base R6 design: it would continue to allow maps whose source cardinalities cannot be interpreted consistently. Keeping `integer` while adding an error invariant would still reject the same invalid negative values, so no materially less-breaking design that meets the enforcement goal was identified.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Warning-only or permissive validation would preserve malformed R4 instances but would not guarantee executable cardinality consistency.

evidence.detail: R4 uses integer min and string max without these local invariants.
R6 uses unsignedInt min and adds smp-2/smp-3 error constraints.
Computed diff showed the new source constraints and min type replacement.

examples.examplesMd: The example illustrates values the R4 element types could carry but R6 forbids. Such values are unlikely to be semantically useful.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 narrows source.min to unsignedInt and adds explicit error constraints for source.max syntax and min/max consistency.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R6 validators fail negative min values, non-numeric non-star max values, and cases where min exceeds numeric max. R4 validators did not have these StructureMap-owned invariants.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Normalize source cardinalities before R6 validation. Remove invalid min/max values if they were not meaningful, or correct them to the intended non-negative cardinality range.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: This is backward compatible for semantically well-formed maps and breaking only for maps that relied on permissive R4 structural validation of nonsensical cardinality values.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R6 tightens source cardinality metadata by making `source.min` an `unsignedInt` and adding error constraints that `min` must not exceed numeric `max`, and that `max` must be `*` or an integer. That can reject R4 instances that were structurally allowed but semantically suspect, such as negative minima, nonnumeric maxima, or `min > max`. This is a real validator behavior change, but it aligns the computable model with the stated meaning of cardinality and avoids executable maps with impossible source occurrence rules.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `StructureMap.group.rule.source.min` is `integer`; `source.max` is `string` with prose `Specified maximum cardinality... - a number or a *`.
R6 StructureDefinition: `source.min` is `unsignedInt`.
R6 constraints `smp-2` and `smp-3` enforce `min <= max` and `max` being an integer or `*`.
Supplied maturity context: R4 StructureMap FMM 2, trial-use.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral. It does not demand preserving malformed cardinality values when the R6 constraint improves consistency of executable map rules.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: some R4 maps that passed structural validation because of loose integer/string typing now fail R6 validation when cardinality values are nonsensical.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: A less-breaking design could make these warnings rather than errors, but that would allow impossible cardinality metadata to remain valid in executable maps. The stricter base invariant is a reasonable safety/computability tradeoff.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree: the existing report correctly identified a validator-tightening break, but the fresh assessment views it as proportionate and mostly limited to bad or ambiguous cardinality values.

findings.title: target.parameter.value[x] adds date, time, and dateTime in R6

oldState.summary: R4 target.parameter.value[x] supports id, string, boolean, integer, and decimal.

newState.summary: R6 target.parameter.value[x] retains the R4 choices and adds date, time, and dateTime.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The type expansion does not break R4 instances moving forward, but R6 maps can contain valueDate, valueTime, or valueDateTime parameters that R4 StructureMap cannot represent. R4-era engines and generated models may not handle these typed literal arguments.

justification.inferredGoal: Add first-class date/time literal support for transform parameters.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: this is a type-domain widening that preserves R4-valid `target.parameter.value[x]` instances.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Adding date, time, and dateTime parameter literals is a reasonable expressivity improvement and does not invalidate R4 instances moving forward to R6. The reported risk is real for R6-to-R4 conversion and older runtimes, but it is not a breaking R4-to-R6 base-design change.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Because all R4 value choices remain valid in R6, no backward-compatible alternative is needed for R4-to-R6 preservation. Encoding date/time literals as strings, using extensions, or rejecting them during downgrade are conversion strategies for R6-to-R4 interoperability, not base R6 alternatives.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The tradeoff is R6-to-R4 downgrade and old-engine support for new date/time choices, not a less-breaking R4-to-R6 base-design issue.

evidence.detail: R4 value[x] choices exclude date/time/dateTime.
R6 value[x] choices include date/time/dateTime.
Computed diff showed the added choice types.

examples.examplesMd: Encoding a date as valueString may preserve lexical text but not the FHIR type.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 expands transform parameter literal support to include date/time datatypes. This is primarily a downgrade and old-engine compatibility risk.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 validation rejects valueDate, valueTime, and valueDateTime under target.parameter. R4-generated code usually lacks those choice branches. R6 validation accepts them.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R6-to-R4 conversion, decide whether a date/time parameter can safely become valueString or whether the map must remain R6-only. Preserve date/time typing for R6-native execution where possible.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: This change does not break existing R4 instances when moving forward to R6, but it expands the valid R6 instance space beyond R4's model.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R6 adds `date`, `time`, and `dateTime` choices to `target.parameter.value[x]`. That is a widening for R4-to-R6 migration: every R4 parameter value type remains available, and old R4 maps are not made invalid by the added choices. A new R6 map that uses one of the added temporal choices may not be representable in an R4-only StructureMap processor, but that is a reverse-direction/new-feature issue rather than a problem with migrating R4 content forward.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `StructureMap.group.rule.target.parameter.value[x]` includes the older set of primitive/complex choices but not `date`, `time`, or `dateTime`.
R6 StructureDefinition: `target.parameter.value[x]` includes added `date`, `time`, and `dateTime` choices.
No R4 element is narrowed or removed by this specific change.
Supplied maturity context: R4 StructureMap FMM 2, trial-use.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use does not materially affect the judgment because the change is additive for forward compatibility.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: only maps that choose the new R6 temporal parameter types have downgrade problems; R4-to-R6 validation is not broken.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: No less-breaking R6 base design is needed. Omitting useful new value types would be more restrictive, and adding them does not invalidate R4 maps.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: disagree: the existing report's reverse-conversion concern is technically real, but as a fresh R4-to-R6 path-level review this additive widening is not a meaningful breaking change.

findings.title: R6 permits groups with no rules and rules without names

oldState.summary: R4 requires every group to contain at least one rule and every rule to have a name.
oldState.narrativeMd: group.rule has min=1 and group.rule.name has min=1.

newState.summary: R6 permits group.rule min=0 and group.rule.name min=0.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 can represent empty groups and anonymous rules.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Loosening cardinality does not invalidate old R4 maps in R6, but R6-valid maps can be structurally invalid in R4. R4-era code may assume at least one rule and a non-null rule.name.

justification.inferredGoal: Support more flexible authoring or partial/incremental map definitions.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: relaxing minimum cardinalities preserves existing R4-valid groups and rules in R6.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Supporting empty groups or anonymous rules may be useful for authoring and partial map definitions, and the base change does not make any R4-valid StructureMap invalid in R6. The compatibility concern is downstream representability in R4, not avoidable R4-to-R6 breakage.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: No less-breaking R4-to-R6 alternative applies because the change is already forward-compatible for R4 instances. Profiles, authoring constraints, or downgrade rejection rules can manage R6 maps that omit rules or names, but those are policy choices for R6-to-R4 conversion and runtime handling.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The material cost is only for R6-to-R4 export and R4-era code assumptions about non-empty groups and named rules.

evidence.detail: R4 requires both rule and rule.name.
R6 makes both optional.
Computed diff showed min cardinality decreasing from 1 to 0.

examples.examplesMd: The shown R6 group has no rule, violating R4 group.rule minimum cardinality. A nameless rule similarly violates R4 rule.name.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 broadens the valid StructureMap authoring space by allowing empty groups and anonymous rules.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 validation fails when group.rule is absent or rule.name is absent. R6 validation allows both. R4-based generated code may have non-null assumptions for these fields.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R6-to-R4 downgrades, reject empty groups or anonymous rules unless a deterministic, semantically safe placeholder can be supplied. Do not invent executable rules just to satisfy R4 cardinality.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: No R4-to-R6 break exists for this change, but it is a material representability and codegen risk for consumers that accept R6 and then emit or process R4.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R6 relaxes required cardinalities for rules and rule names. That means some R6 maps may not downgrade cleanly to R4, but it does not invalidate any R4 map or remove an R4 wire element. Forward migration from R4 to R6 can keep the existing rule names and rules unchanged. Any risk is limited to R4-era tooling making assumptions while consuming new R6 maps, not to the R4-to-R6 compatibility of existing content.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `StructureMap.group.rule` and `StructureMap.group.rule.name` have minimum cardinality 1.
R6 StructureDefinition: the same paths have minimum cardinality 0.
No R4-valid instance becomes invalid because of a minimum-cardinality relaxation.
Supplied maturity context: R4 StructureMap FMM 2, trial-use.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use does not raise concern because the change is relaxing, not tightening, for R4 content moving forward.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: an R6 map that omits rules or rule names may not be expressible as R4, but R4 maps remain valid with respect to this path.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: No less-breaking base design is needed for R4-to-R6. Keeping R6 names mandatory would avoid reverse downgrade loss but would also block the R6 relaxation without preserving any R4 instance that would otherwise fail.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: disagree: the existing report correctly notices a downgrade issue, but its impact framing overstates the relevance to R4-to-R6 compatibility.

findings.title: R6 adds root StructureMap.const for named constant values

oldState.summary: R4 StructureMap has no root const backbone.

newState.summary: R6 adds repeating StructureMap.const with required name and value string children.
newState.narrativeMd: const.name is id and const.value is string.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The optional addition does not invalidate R4 instances in R6. However, R6 maps can depend on root constants that have no standard R4 element, and R4 engines may not resolve those names during transform execution.

justification.inferredGoal: Add a standard place for reusable named constants in map definitions.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: `StructureMap.const` is an optional R6 addition and does not invalidate R4 StructureMap instances.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: A standard place for reusable constants is a reasonable R6 feature, and adding an optional element is forward-compatible for R4-to-R6 validation. The interoperability risk comes from R6 maps that depend on constants when exported to R4 or interpreted by R4-era engines.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Backward-compatible alternative analysis is not applicable to R4-to-R6 preservation because R4 instances without `const` remain valid. R4 export can inline constants or use agreed extensions after semantic review, but those approaches do not change the fact that the base R6 addition itself is not an R4-to-R6 breaking design.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Inlining constants or using extensions can help R6-to-R4 conversion, but those are backport mitigations rather than less-breaking base R6 designs.

evidence.detail: R6 adds the const backbone and required children.
Computed diff showed StructureMap.const added.

examples.examplesMd: A downgrade could inline the value wherever the constant is referenced, but that requires parsing and rewriting the map language, not just reshaping JSON.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 adds first-class map constants. This is a useful new feature, but it expands R6 StructureMap beyond R4's standard representation.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 validation rejects StructureMap.const as an unknown root element. R4 engines that parse only R4 map definitions will not resolve R6 constants unless they implement an extension convention or preprocessing step.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R6-to-R4 conversion, inline constant values or store them in an agreed extension only after verifying every reference site. Prefer keeping maps that rely on const as R6-native when exact behavior matters.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The addition is safe for R4-to-R6 import but creates a non-representable R6 feature for R4 export.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R6 adds an optional root-level `StructureMap.const` backbone for named FHIRPath expressions. This does not make any R4 StructureMap invalid and does not require existing maps to add constants. It is a new R6 authoring feature; the only compatibility issue is that R6 maps using `const` cannot be interpreted by R4-only processors without expansion or transformation. I also did not find the old report's claimed required child burden in the R6 StructureDefinition: the added `const.name` and `const.value` children are optional in the base definition.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: no `StructureMap.const` element.
R6 StructureDefinition: `StructureMap.const` is added as `0..*`.
R6 StructureDefinition: `StructureMap.const.name` and `StructureMap.const.value` are each `0..1`, not required in the base element definition.
Supplied maturity context: R4 StructureMap FMM 2, trial-use.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use has little effect because the change is optional and additive for forward migration.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: R6 maps that rely on `const` need expansion or transformation for R4 processors, but existing R4 maps do not break.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: No less-breaking R6 base design is needed. Adding an optional construct is already the compatibility-preserving way to introduce constants; requiring authors to avoid constants would merely suppress a new feature.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: disagree: the existing report treats the addition as a higher conversion problem and appears to overstate the child cardinalities; the fresh evidence shows an optional additive feature with only reverse/new-feature impact.
